issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: Employ `allows ref struct` in libraries
issue_context.body:
### Background and motivation

C# 13 and .NET 9 now allow generic parameters to be annotated as `where T : allows ref struct`, indicating that the T may be a ref struct (expanding the allowed types that may be used as the `T`, as opposed to normal constraints which require that the `T` be the specified kind). For this to be broadly useful, we need to annotate appropriate library surface area. Any `T` annotated as such is then subject to all the rules of a `ref struct`, and it’s a breaking change to remove the `allows ref struct` anti-constraint, so we can only use it in places where we don’t now or won’t in the future need to store instances of the `T` to the heap. Developers implementing interfaces on `ref struct`s also need to be aware that it’s a breaking change for DIMs to be added to an interface implemented on one without also overriding that DIM at the same time, since the lack of an override would result in boxing the `ref struct` to the interface type.

Is there anything stopping the compiler from heuristically treating type parameters on delegate types (provided they're an input and not otherwise constrained) implicitly as `allows ref struct` at their declaration site? The anti-constraint (or lack thereof) is really only relevant at use-sites where a delegate instance is actually created/consumed.

```cs
var taskType = typeof(Task<>).MakeGenericType(typeof(Action<>).GetGenericArguments()[0]);
Console.WriteLine(taskType);
```

That code compiles and executes successfully, even though it doesn't do anything. It's legal since the generic constraints on `Action<>`'s _TArg_ are no more permissive than the generic constraints on `Task<>`'s _TArg_.

But if `Action<>`'s _TArg_ ever becomes more permissive (e.g., because it now allows ref structs), the reflection APIs will throw an exception in the call to `MakeGenericType`. It's a really weird edge case, and I don't know why somebody would do this with the unbound _TArg_ type instead of a real bound type. But... I guess _technically_ it's a break?

Edit: I'm not arguing that this is undesirable. Just that there might be some bizarre unintended consequences and we should be sure we're ok with them before proceeding.

> Is there anything stopping the compiler from heuristically treating type parameters on delegate types

I remember it was discussed and explicitly denied, to avoid breaking change.

> Just that there might be some bizarre unintended consequences and we should be sure we're ok with them before proceeding.

I expect this is one of those cases where metadata versions over time, where we've always viewed generic constraints becoming more permissive as acceptable, and where we've typically viewed using reflection to be dangerous and prone to breaks. So we should say that this is one of the weird edge cases that ideally no one is doing but which is overall best for the ecosystem to allow to break.

It's also worth noting you could run into the same consideration any of the places where we removed `where T : struct` or `where T : IEquatable<T>` constraints. For example, given some `struct MyStruct<T> where T : struct` and some `struct MyOtherStruct<T> where T : struct`, it would've been valid to do `typeof(MyStruct<T>).MakeGenericType(myOtherStruct.GetType().GetGenericArguments()[0])`. However, if you relax it to be `struct MyOtherStruct<T> { }` (dropping the `where T : struct` constraint), this code can now fail given a `MyOtherStruct<string> myOtherStruct` which is now valid.

> Marshal.SizeOf<T>

Should we omit the legacy interop APIs from this proposal? From user point of view, it is inconsistent for `Marshal.SizeOf<T>` to get the treatment, but `Marshal.PtrToStructure<T>` or `Marshal.DestroyStructure<T>` to be left without the treatment. These APIs are typically used together.

Essentially: 

```csharp
Func<Span<int>, Span<int>> func;
Span<int> M(Span<int> span) => ...
```

Calling `func` or `M` here have the same impacts in terms of lifetime semantics. So situations where a method would need `scoped` it's reasonable to assume we'd want `scoped` in delegates. 

IME: `scoped` is most commonly used in cases that don't line up with our core delegates: 

- Instance members on `struct` where want to differentiate that `this` is being returned but a parameter is not 
- `in / ref` parameters that we want to delineate are not captured in a returned `ref struct`

Basically: this is something I'd consider in the future if we find that the need dictates it.
